## 1. What was read

**891 research articles** from 32 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **296** records (25% of the 1,187 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. Every count below is over the full harvest and is inflated by this; the figure above is not.

!!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: bioinfo +43%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). This month is missing *Nat Mach Intell*. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: Nucleic Acids Res 140, JAMA 124, Nature 101, Bioinformatics 95, Science 89, Genome Biol 49.

## 3. The evidence that moved it










!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This section opened by claiming that the interception thread took **three
    independent hits in one month, all on the same assumption**. On re-reading
    the abstracts, one of the three was a second telling of another and one
    pointed the other way.

    [41528342](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41528342/) has no abstract and no
    named authors: it is a *Cancer Discovery* research-watch restatement of
    [41291291](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41291291/), the *Nature* paper
    published five days earlier and carded separately on this thread. Counting
    both put one study on the interception curve twice; it is now neutral.

    [41380103](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41380103/) was read from its
    title. Its conclusion is that genomics **separates** progressor from
    nonprogressor smoldering myeloma, and it delivers a score, validated on 101
    independent samples, that adds to 20/2/20. It is now carded `supports`.

    One genuine hit survives, and the paragraph below states it.

**Premalignant colorectal lesions are not one clone caught early.**
[41291291](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41291291/) (*Nature*) reports that human premalignant colorectal
lesions are polyclonal in origin. Interception is built on the premise that a
precursor is a single clone caught early, and this says the unit of the thing
being intercepted is not what the field has been modelling. It is one paper, in
one tissue, and it should be carried as one.

**Precursor staging got sharper rather than looser.**
[41380103](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41380103/) (*JCO*) sequences 224 precursor samples, 51 of them
paired with the myeloma the same patient went on to develop, against 1,779
newly diagnosed myelomas. Progressor smoldering myeloma is already genomically
myeloma — over 80% of driver mutations present at both time points, most
progressor samples showing only minor clonal change — while nonprogressor
smoldering myeloma carries a lower mutational load, no chromosome 8 copy-number
alterations and an MGUS-like profile. The genomic score built on that separation
identifies low-risk patients unlikely to progress and adds clinical value on top
of 20/2/20. The assertive title dissolves the old taxonomy; the result underneath
it makes precursor staging more discriminating, not less, which is what
interception needs.

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    The paragraph that follows read: "SERENA-6 is the month's most consequential
    negative, and it is a patient-reported outcome … ctDNA-guided early
    switching produces no patient-perceived quality-of-life gain." That is the
    opposite of what
    [41125211](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41125211/) reports. The card was
    written from the title, which names the trial, the drugs and the population
    and gives no result, and a null was supplied for it. Every reported hazard
    ratio in the abstract favours the switching arm. The argument built on it —
    a surrogate/endpoint gap visible inside the thread's own flagship — has no
    support here and is withdrawn.

**SERENA-6 reported its patient-reported outcomes, and they favour the molecular
trigger.** [41125211](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41125211/) (*Ann Oncol*) reports that switching from aromatase
inhibitor to camizestrant on emergent *ESR1* mutation, with the CDK4/6 inhibitor
continued, delays deterioration in pain (hazard ratio 0.57), dyspnoea (0.52) and
emotional functioning (0.51), alongside the previously reported global health
status hazard ratio of 0.54. SERENA-6 is the trial that made molecular relapse
rather than clinical relapse the trigger for changing therapy, and this is the
result that says patients report the molecularly triggered switch as better, not
only the scan.

**The neuro-immune axis produced two supports and no refutations**, both
mechanistic and both in top general journals: a tumour-brain sensory-sympathetic
axis restraining antitumour immunity ([41639447](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41639447/)), and sensory neurons
driving immune exclusion through dense extracellular matrix
([41650969](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41650969/)). The second is the more useful, because it supplies a
physical mechanism — matrix density — for a thread that has mostly trafficked in
signalling. A third card, [41629655](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41629655/), was counted here as
serotonin driving chemoresistance; it is a *Nature Immunology* research
highlight, single author, no abstract, and the study it summarises is not in this
index. Nothing about that finding can be checked from the record, and it is now
neutral.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

!!! note "Withdrawn from this month 2026-08-27"
    This section carried a blinatumomab / CD19 CAR-T result attributed to
    41643692 in *Lancet Oncology*. That PMID is
    ["Time to act: a global call for oral cancer prevention and early
    detection"](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41643692/) and has nothing to
    do with the claim.

    The finding is real — it is
    [41643192](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41643192/), a single transposed
    digit away, in *Blood*. But it is dated **2026-04**, so it was never a
    February result and cannot stay in this briefing. It has been re-pointed in
    `data/evidence.yml` and belongs to April.

    Every automated check passed this for months: the PMID existed, its date
    matched the index, and its stored title matched the paper. What none of
    them test is whether the card is *about* the paper it cites.

Two cards this month are engineering *around* a failure rather than evidence for
or against a target. [41735000](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41735000/) proposes depleting TIGIT-high
CD226-negative clonal Tregs as a safer route to TIGIT targeting.
[41734999](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41734999/) is a *JITC* commentary on work by Du et al., in which
an Arg1-promoter-driven CD47 CAR macrophage regressed breast and gastric tumours
in mice with minimal erythrocyte toxicity — secondary reporting of another
group's preclinical mouse work, not primary data, and the comparison with the
haematotoxicity that sank the CD47 antibodies is this corpus's inference rather
than the commentary's result. Both are filed as supports on
`next-gen-checkpoints`, but note what they are: the target survives only by
being approached through a different cell or a narrower subset. That is the
same manoeuvre as CD47 reappearing in December 2025 as a CAR-macrophage homing
address rather than a drug.

### (b) Method credibility

[41559218](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41559218/) (*Nat Genet*) is the strongest card of the month:
cell-segmentation error frequently *dominates* differential expression,
neighbourhood and ligand-receptor results in imaging spatial transcriptomics.
Read with January's [41519776](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41519776/), two consecutive months now say the
two most common operations in imaging spatial transcriptomics — deciding where
cells are, and testing which genes differ — are unreliable at the base.

[41601205](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41601205/): reported transcription-factor binding-site accuracy is
an artifact of how the negative set was constructed, not of model capacity.
[41580962](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41580962/): drug-synergy deep models ignore chemical structure
entirely, and one-hot drug identity reproduces their reported performance. These
are the cleanest kind of refutation available — the model is replaced by a
trivial baseline and the number does not move.

[41736096](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41736096/) was carded here as evidence that published
cfDNA-methylation cancer classifiers carry demographic bias inflating their
apparent performance. It says something narrower and more constructive:
demographic imbalance in training data *degrades* performance for minority
populations, and DeBias removes the bias-associated subspaces from the feature
space and improves cancer detection for those populations, with the gains
reproduced in independent cohorts. It makes no claim about the performance of
published classifiers, and it is now neutral.
[41742311](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41742311/): a benchmark of LLM agents on single-cell omics
quantifies where they break down on real workflows — the maturity signal for
`agentic-ai` is the arrival of benchmarks, and it keeps arriving as bad news.
